demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
I feel isolated and set apart from others
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Physical pain in the same body parts as during the event is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being an unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one, unless the patient was also physically injured during the event. That makes this item clinically implausible from the provided trauma context.

A global mistrust appraisal is a weak fit with bereavement trauma unless there is some interpersonal betrayal, negligence, or assault-related context. The rest of the profile centers on loss, alarm, and isolation rather than interpersonal threat from other people, so this item is not well supported by the trauma type or the other selected items.

For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, ambulances can plausibly cue the death context and workplace cues may be idiosyncratically linked, but 'People cycling' is hard to connect clinically unless the loved one died in a cycling-related incident, which is not reflected anywhere else in threat, appraisals, or memory. It stands out as a trigger with no supporting context in the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: The memory profile is dominated by grief-related recall and affective reliving without clear imagery, which fits bereavement trauma. 'Intense shame' on recall is not impossible, but here it lacks support from the negative appraisals, which focus on identity loss, isolation, and life destruction rather than self-blame, guilt, or humiliation. In this profile, shame is insufficiently integrated with the rest of the formulation and trauma type.

vignette: Kofi had always found solace in his work as a painter. The smell of turpentine and oil paints, the feel of a brush in his hand, it all seemed to calm his mind. But that was before his wife, Ama, passed away suddenly. It's been two years now, but Kofi still finds himself waking up in the dead of night, his body tense and ready to react to danger. He can't shake off the feeling of being on guard, even inside his own home. It started with the ambulance that took Ama away. The sound of its sirens still haunts him, making him feel like he's constantly waiting for another tragedy to strike. Whenever he hears an ambulance outside his studio, Kofi's mind starts racing and his body goes into high alert. He tries to distract himself by focusing on his work, but the memories come flooding back - images of Ama's lifeless body, the feeling of emptiness that consumed him. He can't help but wonder if he could have done something to prevent her death. The memories are always there, lurking just beneath the surface. Sometimes Kofi feels like he's drowning in grief, overwhelmed by emotions that he can't quite explain. Other times, it's as if his mind is a blank slate, devoid of any clear images or memories. But the pain is always there, gnawing away at him. Kofi's friends and family have tried to be supportive, but he feels isolated and set apart from others. He struggles to connect with them, to find meaning in a world that seems to have lost all sense. His work, once his passion, now feels like a chore. He goes through the motions, but it's all just a reminder of what he's lost. As Kofi navigates this new reality, he finds himself on edge more often than not. The slightest noise can startle him, and he's constantly looking over his shoulder, waiting for something to go wrong. His body is always tense, ready to react to danger that may or may not be there. And when the memories come flooding back, Kofi feels like he's losing himself all over again. The triggers are everywhere - in the ambulance sirens, in the conversations about loss and grief, even in his own workspace. They bring back the memories, which in turn fuel his feelings of threat and danger. It's a vicious cycle that Kofi can't seem to break free from. He feels like he's lost himself, like his life has been destroyed by the trauma. Despite all this, Kofi still holds onto hope. He hopes that one day he'll find a way to manage his symptoms, to learn to live with the memories without being consumed by them. For now, though, the pain and fear remain, a constant reminder of what he's lost. What brought Kofi to seek help was the realization that he couldn't keep living like this. He wants to be able to connect with others again, to find meaning in his work and his life. Most of all, he wants to be able to remember Ama without feeling overwhelmed by grief and pain.
